transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Emma Liu (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (Redwood Product), Rajiv Kapoor (Marigold Head of ML), Lena Ortiz (Marigold Platform Eng), Mark Chen (Marigold CTO)
Notes/artifacts shared: [Deck: batching-cost-sim-v3.pdf], [Spreadsheet: marigold-cost-model.xlsx], link: https://redwood.app/j/xx-optimizer-sim (shared)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Focus: Optimize console walkthrough; recommended batching and prefix/KV caching strategies; 1M-token cost sim; next steps: pilot.

Topics covered: batching, kv/prefix cache, quantization fallback, Dedicated vs Hosted, latency vs cost tradeoffs.

Transcript body:
[00:00:09] Emma (Redwood AE): Alright thanks everyone for joining, running about 48 minutes today. Quick intros — I'm Emma, I'll handle follow-ups, Diego will do the console walkthrough.
[00:00:18] Rajiv (Marigold): Yep, Rajiv here. We're mainly trying to understand where we get the most unit cost wins — prefix cache, batching — and figure out what a pilot would look like.
[00:00:25] Diego (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Rajiv. Quick note: we already got the prompt distribution Lena uploaded, so we'll use that for the sim. If anything is wrong shout out.
[00:00:35] Lena (Marigold): I uploaded a csv earlier, maybe the file name got mangled in upload, it's marigold_prompt_mix_v2.csv.
[00:00:40] Diego: Got it, I'll pull that. Ok jumping into the Optimize console — if anyone can't see my screen let me know.
[00:00:51] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) can see it.
[00:00:55] Diego: First slide, baseline assumptions: average request length 230 tokens, response length 85 tokens, chat context avg 6 turns, QPS peak ~8 req/s. Baseline model: open-ish 7B variant (we'll call it rwd-instruct-7b) on hosted GPUs, no prefix cache, batching disabled (batch size = 1). Costs: baseline $0.61 per 1k output tokens in this config — (note: rough numbers for demo).
[00:01:30] Mark (Marigold): Wait that cost seems high relative to what we saw with other vendors — is that per token or includes infra?
[00:01:36] Emma: Good callout, that's per 1k output tokens only for the hosted compute; doesn't include S3 storage for prompts or network egress. The spreadsheet we'll share breaks those lines out.
[00:01:48] Diego: Moving on, the Optimize suggestion engine picks batching = 4 for this workload to target latency < 250ms p95 and keep throughput steady. It also recommends enabling prefix cache for first-turn system-like turns (we detect stable prefixes across conversation types).
[00:02:05] Rajiv: Quick Q: how are you detecting stable prefixes? Our chat system sometimes rewrites system prompts per user.
[00:02:11] Diego: Good question — detection uses a heuristic on token n-gram overlap plus a simple ttl for cached keys; we'll surface false positives. You can also provide static prefix anchors via the API to force-candidate.
[00:02:25] Lena: If enabling prefix cache, does KV cache still buy us anything?
[00:02:28] Diego: Yes — prefix cache stores encoded KV pairs for shared leading context. Full KV cache is per-session full past tokens and helps in long context generation; for short multi-turn chat, prefix cache often captures 70–85% of repeated compute. The console's sim estimated 42% token compute saved via prefix cache alone for your dataset.
[00:02:45] Emma: To make that concrete: in the 1M-token sim we ran, baseline cost was ~$620. With batching=4 + prefix cache hits ~0.42, cost dropped to ~$390 — roughly 37% savings. Add a robust KV cache + burst batching to 8 in off-peak we see a 48% reduction in compute cost.
[00:03:12] Rajiv: Those are good numbers. What about latency tail? We're sensitive to 95th percentile since product UX complains.
[00:03:19] Diego: There's a tradeoff. Batching increases throughput and lowers avg cost, but p95 increases slightly if you use static batching windows. Our runtime uses continuous batching with dynamic micro-batches to keep p95 within SLOs. For this workload, p95 went from 210ms baseline to 260ms at batching=4 and 290ms at batching=8. But enabling prefix cache actually reduces p95 because cached KV skips first-attention compute. So combined, batching=4 + prefix cache kept p95 ~230ms in our run.
[00:03:52] Mark: Any fallback options if latency spikes during peak?
[00:03:55] Diego: Yes — routing policy: serve to Dedicated pool or lower-latency model variant (quantized 8-bit) as a fallback. There's a config to set max allowed p95 and auto-failover.
[00:04:05] Lena: Could you show the actual sim?
[00:04:08] Diego: Sure — switching to the simulation tab. Here's the prompt mix applied across the 1M tokens. The console plots token-level cost, cache-hit histogram, and latency distribution.
[00:04:25] [Screen: console graph — cost waterfall, hit-rate histogram]
[00:04:28] Diego: See the left chart: baseline compute dom, middle waterfall shows prefix cache saving slice in green. The right is inferred p95. Note the spike at ~120k tokens where we had a long response (a doc summary) that didn't hit prefix cache — that single class changes averages.
[00:04:45] Rajiv: What's your assumption for model perf when quantized? Loss of quality might be a concern.
[00:04:50] Diego: We annotate quality risk in the sim — for rwd-instruct-7b quantized we estimate a 1-2% drop on our internal evals on instruction tasks. For docs/summarization it's variable. Optimize flags prompts where quantization risk is high and we don't route those to quantized fallback.
[00:05:07] Rajiv: Can we pin by route? For example, ban quant fallback for the 'legal-summary' route.
[00:05:10] Emma: Yes, per-route rollout policy supports allowlist/denylist and weight-based rollouts — you can have quant only for low-risk routes.
[00:05:18] Mark: Security/compliance — if we consider Private deployment, how does caching behave? We need KMS and audit logs.
[00:05:24] Priya (Redwood Product): In Private mode the control plane is in your VPC, KV/prefix caches can be configured to use your HSM or KMS for keying. Audit events for cache hits/misses and rollout decisions can be exported to your SIEM. We'll share the SOC2/KMS one-pager after this.
[00:05:37] Lena: That helps. Another practical question: warmup. If we enable prefix cache, do we need to pre-warm caches to get benefits?
[00:05:44] Diego: Pre-warm is recommended for fresh deployments. You can run a warmup job that replays historical prompts to populate cache; Optimize provides a warmup job template — this is what we included in the spreadsheet. For ongoing traffic, cache warms quickly for stable prefixes.
[00:05:58] Rajiv: Ok show me the spreadsheet numbers — the marigold-cost-model.xlsx?
[00:06:02] Diego: Opening the shared sheet — column A has prompt class, B avg tokens, C freq, D simulated hit-rate. For class "support-chat" we show 0.48 prefix hit, "billing" 0.66, "legal-summary" 0.05.
[00:06:19] Rajiv: That matches our intuition — legal-summary very variable so low hit.
[00:06:22] Diego: The bottom line sim shows three scenarios: Hosted baseline $620, Hosted + batching+prefix ~$390, Hosted + batching+prefix + quant fallback ~$325, Dedicated reserved + batching/prefetch (amortized instance cost) ~$290. These are all compute-only estimates.
[00:06:43] Mark: Dedicated requires a minimum commitment, how big is the pool for our QPS?
[00:06:48] Emma: For your peak QPS ~8 req/s with avg tokens, our prescriptive minimum is a 2-GPU pool (A100 class or similar) with autoscale policies and burst capacity. We'll include cost amortization in the term sheet.
[00:06:59] Rajiv: A few nitty gritty items: 1) How often do prefix caches expire? 2) How do you version model kernels?
[00:07:06] Diego: 1) TTL configurable per-prefix, default 24 hours but can be tuned to minutes for high-churn. 2) Model kernel selection is done at load-time; runtime can hot-swap between kernel variants for quant vs fp16, and we keep versioned model artifacts so rollouts are deterministic.
[00:07:20] Lena: Any monitoring hooks? We need to alert when cache-hit drops, or when p95 spikes after a rollout.
[00:07:24] Diego: Console emits metrics: prefix_hit_rate, kv_hit_rate, p50/p95 latencies per route, cost per token by route. You can set threshold alerts and have automatic rollback on degraded quality via eval hooks.
[00:07:36] Rajiv: Let's talk pilot. Ideally we want a 2-week pilot where Redwood runs the sim on our actual traffic then we run a small Dedicated trial with warmup and compare.
[00:07:45] Emma: That matches our standard pilot. Steps: you share prompt distribution (Lena), we run the 1M-token sim and a 48-hour live warmup on a sandbox pool, then we compare cost and p95. If you like the results, we move to reserved Dedicated or Private.
[00:07:58] Mark: Any red flags?
[00:08:00] Diego: Risk areas: quantization for high-stakes routes, cache warmup time for very low-frequency prefixes, and ensuring keys/KMS are set up for Private. None look like showstoppers.
[00:08:09] Rajiv: Cool. Walk me through an example of a cache miss causing tail latency — just want to see raw logs.
[00:08:13] Diego: Sure — switching to traces. This is a trace from a long-doc summary that had no prefix hit. You'll see full attention compute at the start and a 1.8x token compute cost on that request. Trace shows timestamps at every 128-token chunk, and we annotate kernel selection.
[00:08:34] [Diego shares trace snippet — occasional transcription glitch: 'kernal' as spoken]
[00:08:39] Lena: Those per-chunk timings are great. We'll look for patterns to maybe rewrite prompts to create reusable prefixes.
[00:08:46] Emma: Quick recap before we close — Diego will run the 1M-token sim and share traces and the console link; I will send the pricing/Dedicated term and SOC2/KMS doc; Lena will share prompt distribution; Rajiv to confirm pilot stakeholders and timeline.
[00:08:58] Mark: Sounds good.
[00:09:00] [End of recorded portion — remaining time used for off-record pricing Q&A between Emma and Rajiv (not transcribed)]

Notes about transcription imperfections: speaker labels occasionally mis-attributed, 'kernel' sometimes transcribed as 'kernal', model name obfuscated as rwd-instruct-7b or similar, timestamps approximate.
